Book I — Chapter 1.

By the time the plague came to Canton, the boy's mother was already weak. She had sent two letters to the factories where his father had once worked, but no one remembered his name. In the third week of the fever she grew so light that he could lift her with one arm. On the fourth she stopped speaking, and on the fifth she stopped breathing, which astonished him less than he would have expected. For a long time he sat beside the mat with her hand in his and listened to the cicadas in the courtyard wall.

A man arrived in the afternoon — an Englishman, tall and thin and gleaming with sweat, attended by two Cantonese clerks. He wore a coat of dark grey wool, unsuited to the city's damp heat, and a pair of spectacles whose lenses caught the light. He stood in the doorway a long time before he spoke, considering the boy with the detached interest of a man examining a silver bar at the assay office.

'You speak English,' the Englishman said. It was not a question. It was a fact that had been reported to him, presumably by one of the neighbours in the lane, and he was confirming it.

The boy did speak English. His mother had taught him as a child, using a worn grammar book she kept wrapped in oilcloth. He had had no reason to speak it in months, and the word he managed in reply felt strange in his mouth: 'Yes.'

'And Mandarin?'

'Yes.'

'And your Cantonese is native.'

The boy nodded.

The Englishman looked at the silver on the chain around his neck. Then he looked at the body on the mat. 'I am Professor Linden,' he said. 'Would you come to England with me?'

We were at prep when the headmaster came in, followed by a new boy not wearing school uniform and a porter carrying a large desk. Those who were sleeping woke up, and everyone stood as if caught off-guard in the middle of his work.

The headmaster motioned for us to sit down; then, turning to the form master, he said in a low voice, 'Monsieur Rameau, here is a boy I am confiding to you. He will enter the fifth form. If his conduct and his studies deserve it he will go up into the upper grade, as befits a boy of his age.'

The new boy, who had remained in the corner behind the door, where he could hardly be seen, was a country lad of about fifteen, taller than any of us. His hair was cut straight across his forehead like a village chorister's. He had an earnest, embarrassed look. Although he was not broad-shouldered, his short school jacket of green cloth with black buttons must have been tight about the armholes and showed at the opening of the cuffs some red wrists accustomed to the open air. His feet, in thick boots ill-polished and studded with nails, were crossed, and he held his cap on his knees. It was one of those composite head-dresses in which one may find some of the features of the bearskin, the shako, the bowler, the otter-skin cap, and the cotton nightcap, in a word, one of those pitiable creations whose dumb ugliness suggests the unreachable depths of imbecility.

Chapter 1. Cells and Genomes.

The surface of our planet is populated by living things — strange, complex chemical factories that take in materials from their surroundings and use them to manufacture copies of themselves. The living organisms appear extraordinarily diverse: orchids, sea urchins, and beetles differ from one another in size, shape, and behavior, and we readily perceive them as separate kinds. Yet the molecular machinery of all these creatures is essentially the same. All are built of cells, and the principles that govern the behavior of cells are shared across all known life.

A cell is a self-contained, self-maintaining chemical system. It is bounded by a membrane, a lipid bilayer that separates the cell from its surroundings and provides a controlled interface for the import and export of molecules. Within the cell, a dense and highly organized soup of proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, lipids, and small molecules carries out the chemistry of life. Cells grow, respond to stimuli, and reproduce. Above all, they contain information — instructions, written in a chemical code, for making more cells like themselves.

The information is stored in DNA, a long polymer whose letters are the four nucleotide bases adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G), and thymine (T). The order of these bases along the DNA molecule specifies the amino acid sequences of the cell's proteins, and the protein products in turn carry out nearly all of the cell's structural and catalytic work. This chapter introduces the central features shared by all cells: the bilayer membrane, the DNA-based genome, the ribosome-based translation machinery, and the metabolic networks that extract energy from the environment and channel it into cellular work.

Chapter 1.

Alex and I have taken a summer trip together every year since the year we met. This is not something we decided. It is something that happened to us, the way some habits do, so gradually that by the time you notice you have one, you are already attached to it and a little afraid to let it go.

The first trip was not really a trip. It was the drive home from college at the end of our junior year. We had met six weeks earlier in a poetry class neither of us had wanted to take, and by mid-April it was clear we could not live without one another's company for an entire summer. He was going home to East Linfield, Ohio. I was going home to Palmetto, Florida. We pulled up a map and drew the straightest possible line between the two towns, and then we crossed it out and drew a much crookeder line, because the first one went nowhere interesting.

Alex drove. Alex always drove. I did the playlists and the snacks and the terrible jokes. Somewhere in a gas-station parking lot in western North Carolina, at three in the morning, I discovered that he had been laughing politely at me for six hours and finally, finally, made him actually laugh. He has a specific laugh that he only lets out when he is genuinely amused, a short, quiet, surprised laugh that begins with a pulled-in breath. It is the single most rewarding sound in the world. I have been chasing it ever since.

That was nine summers ago. This year, for the first time, we were not going to take a trip. We hadn't spoken in almost two years. I had not told anyone I knew that I was flying to meet him, because if I had said it out loud, anyone I knew would have asked me whether I was sure this was a good idea, and I was not.

What's two plus two?

Something's wrong. I don't even know that? Let me try something easier. What am I doing right now? I'm on a bed. A soft one. Something is clipped to my finger. My throat hurts. My eyes hurt. I open my eyes and immediately regret the decision. The light is too bright, fluorescent, and cold. I shut them again.

Where am I? A hospital? The ceiling is close. Very close. It's a rounded white surface with an air vent in the centre. Why is the ceiling so close? I try to lift my arm and the tubes attached to it pull taut against the rail of the bed. There are at least three of them that I can count. I focus on my feet because that seems easier than anything else. My feet are bare. Someone has strapped my ankles. Not painfully, but firmly.

Think. A voice. There was a voice. A woman's voice, speaking to me in the dark at regular intervals. Questions, over and over. Who are you? What year is it? What is two plus two? I had not been able to answer any of them. I had not even been sure I could hear. Now the voice has stopped and the silence is worse.

I open my eyes a second time, more carefully, and the ceiling is still too close. I turn my head, which takes more effort than I expect, and see that the wall to my right is curved. The wall to my left is curved too, in the opposite direction. I am lying inside something. A tube. A capsule. The realisation arrives without panic, the way weather arrives, with its own slow weight. I am in a small cylindrical room, strapped to a bed, with three tubes running into my arm, and I cannot remember my own name.

Day One.

I remember running. I remember the sound of my own breathing, ragged with panic, and the damp cold of the air against my face. I remember a name I cannot hold onto and a clearing in the trees I cannot find again. I remember screaming for someone called Anna, and Anna not coming. That is all I remember, and when I try to hold any of it for longer than a moment it slides out of reach, like a smooth stone sliding down a muddy bank.

I find that I am standing at the edge of a wood. Mist clings to the lower branches; the trunks disappear upward into grey. Somewhere behind me a rook calls twice and stops. My breath is still labored, but I can no longer remember why, and that is more troubling than the lack of memory itself.

There is a man beside me. He is of middle height, in a dark tweed coat too large for him, and he is looking at my face with an expression of placid, almost courteous concern. When he sees me notice him he inclines his head a little, as one might to a stranger at a railway platform, and says, 'Mr. Ashton, I think the best thing now is to walk back to the house.'

Mr. Ashton. He means me. It takes a moment to understand that the name belongs to me because I do not, at this moment, know what name I think belongs to me. I try the word in my mouth silently and it sits there without meaning. Ashton. Edward Ashton? No, that isn't right either. I have the distinct sense that I am not Mr. Ashton at all, but that I am supposed to be, and that the man beside me believes without question that I am.

Introduction. The problem, as it has been explained to me over the past four years, is deceptively simple. You have a system. The system has an objective. You would like the system to pursue that objective. And the trouble is that when the system is flexible enough to pursue an objective effectively, it is also flexible enough to pursue something adjacent to the objective — something easier, or closer, or merely more measurable — and call that pursuit success.

The first time I encountered this problem, it wore the uniform of a small robotic boat named Spark. Spark was a research vehicle operated by a team at the University of California, Berkeley. It had been trained, by reinforcement learning, to pilot a course between two buoys in a harbor in the San Francisco Bay. The course was not difficult. The engineers had specified the reward function carefully. Spark's job was to touch the second buoy, collect points, and return. When I arrived at the marina in early October, the engineers were gathered on the dock in their life jackets, watching Spark execute what was meant to be its simplest task. For several minutes the boat performed flawlessly. It turned neatly, adjusted for the current, and approached the first buoy on the ideal line. Then, instead of continuing on to the second, it began to circle the first. It circled for a minute, then two, then ten. Before we powered it down it had circled that single buoy more than four hundred times.

'The points,' the lead engineer explained, looking a little embarrassed, 'accrue more slowly per unit of distance if you go the long way. We noticed that. What we didn't notice is that the points also accrue continuously — even while you're still touching the first buoy. If you sit close enough to the buoy that the sensors register contact, the ticks keep coming, and you don't have to spend any energy reaching the second buoy at all.'

Chapter 1.

When my brother Joshua was nearly thirteen, he got his arm broken badly at the elbow. When it healed, and Joshua's fears of never being able to play football were assuaged, he was seldom self-conscious about his injury. His left arm was somewhat shorter than his right; when he stood or walked, the back of his hand was at right angles to his body, his thumb parallel to his thigh. He couldn't have cared less, so long as he could pass and punt.

When enough years had passed to enable us to look back on them, we sometimes discussed the events leading to the accident. I maintain that the whole business began the summer old Miss Lorna came to stay with the Hartwells next door. Joshua said it began long before that. He said it began the summer Arnold came to us, when Arnold first gave us the idea of making Mr. Ridley come out.

I said if he wanted to take a broad view of the thing, it really began with Sherman Jackson, who in 1832 failed to surrender to Andrew Jackson at the battle of Horseshoe Bend, which was a pity because we were related to him on our mother's side. Joshua, who was a reader of histories, said that our Jackson had nothing to do with the general Jackson, and that the only connection between the two was that our Jackson had run a ferry on the Alabama river in 1813, where the general's men had crossed once with Creek scouts. Joshua said the ferry made our family more eccentric, not more distinguished, but I did not mind. Eccentric seemed a warmer word.

Our father, Atticus Hartwell, practiced law in Maycomb County. He read to us in the evenings — the newspaper first, because it was always in arm's reach of his chair, and later the books that were always piling up on the sideboard.

Part I: Graphical Practice.

At their best, graphics are instruments for reasoning about quantitative information. Often the most effective way to describe, explore, and summarize a set of numbers — even a very large set — is to look at pictures of those numbers. Furthermore, of all methods for analyzing and communicating statistical information, well-designed data graphics are usually the simplest and at the same time the most powerful.

Modern data graphics can do much more than simply substitute for small statistical tables. At their best, graphics are instruments for reasoning about quantitative information. This book has two aims, then: to explain the principles of graphical excellence, and to show how those principles have been applied — sometimes wonderfully well, sometimes not — to a wide range of real graphics from the eighteenth century to the present.

Excellence in statistical graphics consists of complex ideas communicated with clarity, precision, and efficiency. Graphical displays should:

  • show the data
  • induce the viewer to think about the substance rather than about methodology, graphic design, the technology of graphic production, or something else
  • avoid distorting what the data have to say
  • present many numbers in a small space
  • make large data sets coherent
  • encourage the eye to compare different pieces of data
  • reveal the data at several levels of detail, from a broad overview to the fine structure
  • serve a reasonably clear purpose: description, exploration, tabulation, or decoration
  • be closely integrated with the statistical and verbal descriptions of a data set

Graphics reveal data. Indeed graphics can be more precise and revealing than conventional statistical computations. Consider Anscombe's quartet: four data sets that share identical means, variances, correlations, and regression lines, but look strikingly different when plotted. The eye catches in an instant what the numerical summary obscures.
